extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners; patent prosecutors and applicants (patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for evaluating whether a patent application specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph, including examiner procedures for making a prima facie case and assessing original, new, and amended claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (separate from enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and the first paragraph of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 require that the “specification shall contain a written description of the invention ....” This requirement is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to convey that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter and to inform the public what is claimed. Citations: Ariad (en banc), Vas‑Cath, Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle, Capon v. Eshhar. Rejections must be based on substantive law even though Guidelines assist examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of detail to show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession alone does not cure lack of written description. This is a fact‑based inquiry varying with the nature of the invention (Enzo Biochem, Moba, Vas‑Cath).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of showing possession (words/structures/figures/formulas)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant shows that the inventor was in possession by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using such descriptive means as words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: structural chemical formulas, drawings, descriptive words. Lockwood; possession may be shown by actual reduction to practice or by showing the invention was 'ready for patenting'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice or 'ready for patenting' disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by description of an actual reduction to practice, or by showing that the invention was 'ready for patenting' such as by the disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas that show the invention was complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Pfaff; Eli Lilly; Amgen. For biological materials, a deposit may be relevant (see separate rubric) but is not a substitute for written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological material deposits do not substitute for written description
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposit may satisfy the written description requirement with respect to a claimed material in certain circumstances, but such a deposit is not a substitute for a written description of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposits must permit verification of identity and characteristics; written description of the deposited material needs to be as complete as possible because examination proceeds on the written disclosure (Enzo Biochem; 37 CFR 1.801 et seq.; Deposit of Biological Materials rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original specification and originally‑filed claims as potential description
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory description may be found in originally‑filed claims or any other portion of the originally‑filed specification; however, not all originally‑filed claims necessarily have adequate written support in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must examine the specification and drawings to assess support for claims (In re Koller, In re Gardner, In re Wertheim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact‑based, case‑by‑case inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with the written description requirement is essentially a fact‑based inquiry that will 'necessarily vary depending on the nature of the invention claimed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations include nature of the invention, amount of knowledge imparted to skilled artisans, and whether the specification reasonably conveys possession (Enzo Biochem, Vas‑Cath).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of adequacy for original claims but examiner's initial burden
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; however, the PTO (examiner) has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make a prima facie case, the examiner must identify claim limitations not adequately supported and explain why (In re Wertheim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim as a whole analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers; claim construction is essential and each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include preamble language and the transitional phrase; consider the import of preamble and transitional terms such as 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of' (In re Katz; Genentech v. Chiron; PPG).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate sufficiency of structures, acts, or functions recited
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should evaluate each claim to determine if sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given the preamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of definitions or details for well‑established terms should not be the basis for a written description rejection; determine whether limitations are structural or functional in context (Bell Communications Research; Corning Glass).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims require description of the combination (not just elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim drawn to a particular combination of elements may be unsupported even if the specification lists each element separately, where there is inadequate description of the particular combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must clearly and specifically explain why the specification does not support the claimed combination (Hyatt v. Dudas; Stored Value Solutions example). Burden then shifts to applicant to point out support or amend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function‑only or method‑of‑making descriptions may be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention described solely in terms of a method of making and/or its function may lack written descriptive support where there is no described or art‑recognized correlation between the disclosed function and the structure(s) responsible for the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: amino acid sequence vs. naturally occurring DNA/mRNA; processes that do not put inventor in possession of product structure (In re Bell; In re Deuel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus/species disclosure limits — laundry list problem
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'laundry list' disclosure of every possible moiety does not necessarily constitute a written description of every species in a genus because it would not 'reasonably lead' those skilled in the art to any particular species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genus disclosure may not support claims to a subgenus or specific species without adequate particularity (Fujikawa; In re Ruschig; In re Lukach; Purdue Pharma v. Faulding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that encompass unstated structures/elements may lack support
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may read on additional structures (e.g., promoters, coding regions) beyond a disclosed sequence; although a sequence may be disclosed, there may be insufficient description of other structures embraced by the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: 'A gene comprising SEQ ID NO:1.' Consider whether other structures are adequately described; see MPEP § 2106 for subject matter eligibility guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: New or amended claims must be supported by original disclosure (no new matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: New or amended claims which introduce elements or limitations that are not supported by the as‑filed disclosure violate the written description requirement and the proscription against new matter (35 U.S.C. 132 and 251).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support may be express, implicit, or inherent. Applicant may amend spec to include originally claimed material. See In re Rasmussen, In re Benno, In re Smith. Examiner should require applicant to point to support; a simple statement may suffice in some cases (MPEP refs).

rubrics_metrics.name: No in haec verba requirement; obvious error corrections permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: While there is no in haec verba (word‑for‑word) requirement, amendments to correct an obvious error do not constitute new matter where the ordinary artisan would recognize the error and its appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sequencing errors in nucleic acid sequences may be corrected when conforming to deposited material and following 37 CFR 1.804 requirements (In re Oda; Cubist v. Hospira).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposits after filing to support sequence corrections — conditions apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposits made after the filing date may be relied upon to provide support for the correction of sequence information only if applicant submits a statement in compliance with 37 CFR 1.804 stating that the deposited biological material is the biological material specifically defined in the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Cubist Pharm. example and 37 CFR requirements; post‑filing deposits are not a free‑standing cure for lack of written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an essential limitation raises written description issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of a limitation can raise an issue whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention; a claim that omits matter disclosed to be essential may not comply with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: PIN/NIP v. Platte Chem., Gentry Gallery v. Berkline, Johnson Worldwide v. Zebco, Tronzo v. Biomet. If spec states a feature is 'the only possible location' or 'essential', omitting it in claim can be fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description sufficiency may overlap with enablement/indefiniteness issues
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim which omits matter disclosed to be essential may also be subject to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as not enabling or under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite; written description, enablement, and definiteness can be related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: In re Mayhew; In re Venezia; In re Collier. See MPEP § 2172.01 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner prima facie methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a prima facie case of lack of written description, the examiner must identify the claim limitations that are not adequately supported, and explain why the claim is not fully supported by the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear and specific explanation (Hyatt v. Dudas example). For amended/new claims, indicate that applicant should point to where support exists or the examiner will explain why disclosure does not convey possession. Burden shifts to applicant after prima facie showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant response burden for new/amended claims
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to newly added or amended claims, applicant should show support in the original disclosure for the new or amended claims; if applicant points out where support exists and the examiner still finds lack of possession, the examiner has the initial burden of presenting reasoning as to why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP references (2163.04, 2163.06, 714.02). A 'simple statement' may suffice in some contexts; otherwise examiner should explain deficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation of claims in view of specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must be given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction affects written description analysis; consider transitional phrases and claim language import. Cases: In re Katz; In re Morris; Corning; Genentech; PPG.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional disclosure of software and best mode considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: When software constitutes part of a best mode of carrying out an invention, disclosure of functions may suffice because writing code is normally within the skill of the art and does not require undue experimentation; flow charts or source code listings are not always required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fonar Corp. v. Gen. Elec. supports that function disclosure can satisfy best mode for software when coding is within skill of the art. However, assess predictability and skill in art for enablement/written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of level of skill and predictability in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description issues depend on the knowledge and level of skill in the art and whether those skilled in the art would have been permitted to immediately envisage the claimed product arising from the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the art is unpredictable, broader or genus claims may require more detailed disclosure. See Fujikawa, Purdue Pharma examples.
